title: Troubleshooting
text:
Problem
What to do




Read-only file system or permission denied
You tried to write inside course-material. Write to your home folder, ~/pet_course, instead.


The browser shows an error at /proxy/3838/
Check that the app says Listening on, that you used your own port number, and that the address ends with /.


The app says the port is in use and picks another one
Another app is still running. Use the new port number.


The plots in a report don’t respond
Click Trust HTML at the top of the report.


You can’t get bloodstream or PETFit to start
As a fallback, run /neurodesktop-storage/course-material/pet/scripts/run_bloodstream.sh, or /neurodesktop-storage/course-material/pet/scripts/run_petfit.sh followed by regiondef, modelling_plasma, or modelling_ref. They run the same command and print the link to open.


DATA or SIF seem empty
You opened a new terminal. Set the two variables again, as in part 3.


ezBIDS says Select Directory requires Chrome or Edge, or it shows your laptop’s files
You opened ezBIDS in your own browser or in Firefox. Close it, and start it with open_ezbids.sh in a terminal on the Desktop, as in part 1.


A page says “Token authentication is enabled”
This browser isn’t logged in. Open your full Neurodesk link, with ?token=, in this browser first.


The terminal or the browser stops responding
The VPN may have dropped. Reconnect, and open your Neurodesk link again. Your files are kept.

title: PET data analysis workshop
text:
In this workshop, you take PET data from the raw files to estimated outcomes:
You work in your own Neurodesk session on the course server. Everything you create goes in your home folder. The course data are read-only, so you can’t break anything for anyone else.
Start with Before you start.

title: PET data analysis workshop
text:
The dataset
Most of the workshop uses [11C]MC1, a radioligand for cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2), from OpenNeuro dataset ds004869. It has two groups of healthy participants:









Group
Participants
Sessions
Scan length




Blocking
sub-01 to sub-10
baseline, and blocked after 600 mg celecoxib, a COX-2 inhibitor
120 min


Test-retest
sub-11 to sub-27
test and retest
90 min



Every scan has arterial blood data: plasma and whole-blood radioactivity, and the parent fraction measured with HPLC.
In the workshop, you analyse six participants: sub-02, sub-05, and sub-08 from the blocking group, and sub-11, sub-13, and sub-14 from the test-retest group.
For the BIDS conversion in part 1, you use a separate set of raw DICOM files: [11C]PE2I, [18F]FE-PE2I, and [15O]water PET, and a T1-weighted MRI, from two participants.

text:

title: 4. Kinetic modelling with PETFit
text:
PETFit fits kinetic models to regional TACs. It works in two steps: first you define your regions, and then you fit models. You do two analyses: a primary analysis, where you fit the two-tissue compartment model (2TCM) to a few regions, and a second analysis for the Lassen plot, where you fit linear models to more regions.
If this is a new terminal, set the two variables from part 3 first:

title: 4. Kinetic modelling with PETFit
text:
Define your regions
PETPrep extracts TACs from about 100 small FreeSurfer regions. You combine them into larger regions. Define all the regions that you need for both analyses now:

The frontal, temporal, parietal, and occipital cortices. To find which FreeSurfer labels belong to each lobe, see the lobe mapping on the FreeSurfer cortical parcellation page.
The anterior cingulate cortex and the insula.
The hippocampus and the amygdala.


Start the region definition app:
cd ~/pet_course
apptainer run -B $DATA:/data:ro $SIF/petfit.sif --func regiondef --bids_dir /data --derivatives_dir ~/pet_course/derivatives
Open http://130.238.147.132:YOUR_PORT/proxy/3838/ in a browser tab.
Define your regions.
Generate the combined TACs. This takes a couple of minutes, because it combines the TACs for every participant in the dataset.

Your regions and the combined TACs are saved in ~/pet_course/derivatives/petfit.

title: 4. Kinetic modelling with PETFit
text:
Primary analysis: 2TCM

Start the modelling app. It uses the input functions from your own bloodstream models:
cd ~/pet_course
apptainer run -B $DATA:/data:ro $SIF/petfit.sif --func modelling_plasma --bids_dir /data --derivatives_dir ~/pet_course/derivatives --blood_dir ~/pet_course/derivatives/bloodstream/Secondary_Analysis
Open http://130.238.147.132:YOUR_PORT/proxy/3838/ in a browser tab.
On the Data Definition tab, restrict the analysis to the six workshop participants, 02;05;08;11;13;14, and choose two or three of your regions. Create the analysis data.
Read the data definition report. Is anything wrong with the data? If so, revise your data definition and create the analysis data again.
On the Weights Definition and Fit Delay tabs, choose your settings, run each step, and read its report.
On the Model 1 tab, choose 2TCM, fit the model, and read the report.

The reports are in ~/pet_course/derivatives/petfit/Primary_Analysis/reports. Open them in JupyterLab and click Trust HTML.

Does the 2TCM fit the data well?
How do the VT values compare between the baseline and blocked scans? In which regions?

title: 4. Kinetic modelling with PETFit
text:
Lassen analysis: MA1 and Logan
For the Lassen plot, you need VT in more regions. Linear models are faster than the 2TCM and more robust to noise, so you use multilinear analysis 1 (MA1) and the Logan plot. Both estimate VT, and both need a time point, t*, after which the linear relationship holds.

Start the modelling app again, with a new analysis folder:
cd ~/pet_course
apptainer run -B $DATA:/data:ro $SIF/petfit.sif --func modelling_plasma --bids_dir /data --derivatives_dir ~/pet_course/derivatives --blood_dir ~/pet_course/derivatives/bloodstream/Secondary_Analysis --analysis_foldername Lassen_Analysis
Open the app as before.
On the Data Definition tab, choose the same participants, and all the regions that you defined. Create the analysis data, and check the report.
Choose your weights and delay settings, as in the primary analysis.
On the Find t* tab, generate the t* plots, and choose a value of t*.
Fit MA1 as Model 1 and Logan as Model 2, using your value of t*.

The reports are in ~/pet_course/derivatives/petfit/Lassen_Analysis/reports.

How did you choose t*?
How do the VT values from MA1 and Logan compare with each other, and with the 2TCM values from your primary analysis?

title: 4. Kinetic modelling with PETFit
text:
Surface-based analysis with PETSurfer
PETPrep can also run surface-based analyses with PETSurfer, which fits models at each point on the cortical surface instead of in regions. The PETSurfer outputs for this dataset have one report per session:
/neurodesktop-storage/course-material/pet/scripts/view_petsurfer.sh sub-01_ses-baseline.html
The script prints a link. Open it in a new browser tab. To see a list of all reports, run the script without a filename.

What can a surface-based analysis show that a region-based analysis can’t?
What are the costs of working at this level of detail?

title: 2. PETPrep
text: PETPrep preprocesses PET data. It corrects for head motion, registers the PET images to the participant’s MRI, and extracts time-activity curves (TACs) from FreeSurfer regions. A full run takes hours per participant, so you look at outputs that have already been computed for this dataset.

title: 2. PETPrep
text:
2.1 Look at the PETPrep outputs

The reports
PETPrep writes one HTML report per participant. To open a report, run:
/neurodesktop-storage/course-material/pet/scripts/view_petprep.sh sub-01.html
The script prints a link. Open it in a new browser tab. When you are done, press Ctrl+C in the terminal. To see a list of all reports, run the script without a filename.
While you read the reports, think about these questions:

How would you check that the PET-to-MRI registration worked?
What do the motion estimates tell you?
Which outputs would you use for kinetic modelling?



The output files
The outputs are in ~/pet_course/derivatives/petprep. Open one participant’s folder. For example, find the TAC file sub-01_ses-baseline_desc-preproc_seg-gtm_tacs.tsv and open it in JupyterLab. What do the rows and columns contain?

title: 2. PETPrep
text:
2.2 Explore the PETPrep options
You don’t run PETPrep in this workshop. Instead, you install petprep-docker, a Python wrapper that builds the full command to run PETPrep in a container, and you explore its options.
pip install --user petprep-docker
petprep-docker --help
You can ignore the pip warning that ~/.local/bin isn’t on your PATH.
Read through the help text to get an overview of what you can change. In the slides, you then see examples of PETPrep runs that went wrong. For each example, look through the options and work out what you could do differently to make the run work.

title: 1. Convert data to BIDS with ezBIDS
text: ezBIDS is a web app that converts raw scanner data, such as DICOM files, to BIDS. It guesses what each scan is and proposes BIDS names, and you check and correct its guesses before it converts the data. For PET, it uses the same converter as PET2BIDS.

title: 1. Convert data to BIDS with ezBIDS
text:
The raw data
You convert DICOM files from two participants, ASPC0230_06 and ASPC0230_07. Each participant has four scans:

a T1-weighted MRI
[11C]PE2I, a dopamine transporter radioligand
[18F]FE-PE2I, a fluorine-18 version of the same radioligand
[15O]water, for blood flow

The data are in /neurodesktop-storage/course-material/pet/data/sourcedata. They stay on the server: you don’t download them.

title: 1. Convert data to BIDS with ezBIDS
text:
Open ezBIDS
ezBIDS needs a Chrome-type browser to select a folder, and it must run on the server so that it can see the data. So you open it in Chromium on the Neurodesk Desktop.

In JupyterLab, open the Launcher tab and open the Desktop.
On the Desktop, open a terminal, and type:
/neurodesktop-storage/course-material/pet/scripts/open_ezbids.sh
Chromium opens with ezBIDS. The first start can take a minute.







WarningNo copy and paste on the Desktop



Copy and paste doesn’t work on the Desktop, so type the command. Tab completes each part: type /neu, press Tab, type cou, press Tab, and so on.


If the Desktop has a low resolution, open the control panel at the left edge, select settings, and set Scaling mode to Remote resizing.

title: 1. Convert data to BIDS with ezBIDS
text:
Convert the data

Click Select Directory, choose /neurodesktop-storage/course-material/pet/data/sourcedata, and allow ezBIDS to view the files. The upload takes a few minutes.
Check the information that ezBIDS found about the dataset and the participants.
Go through the list of scans. For each scan, check the proposed BIDS name, and correct anything that looks wrong.
Add the information that the converter can’t find in the DICOM files.
Convert the data, and save the BIDS dataset. It stays in your Neurodesk.

While you work, think about these questions:

How many participants does ezBIDS think there are? Is it right? What did it base that on?
For each PET scan, does the tracer that ezBIDS reports match the scan’s series description?
Which information in a PET-BIDS sidecar did the scanner provide, and which did you have to add? What about the injected radioactivity?
Where would blood data fit in this dataset?

title: 1. Convert data to BIDS with ezBIDS
text:
Backup: BIDS-Manager
If ezBIDS doesn’t work, use BIDS-Manager instead. It also runs on the Neurodesk Desktop.

On the Desktop, open a terminal and run:
/neurodesktop-storage/course-material/pet/bids-manager/run_bidsmgr.sh
On the Home tab, create a new dataset project. Save it in your home folder, for example ~/my_bids. Don’t choose a folder inside course-material, which is read-only.
Point BIDS-Manager at the raw data in /neurodesktop-storage/course-material/pet/data/sourcedata.
Scan the raw folder, inspect the proposed names, convert the data, and validate the result.

title: 3. Blood data with bloodstream
text:
bloodstream models arterial blood data and produces an arterial input function for each PET scan. You choose a model for each blood component in an app, and bloodstream fits the models and writes a report.
You run bloodstream twice. First you run it with the default settings, and then you fit models that you choose yourself.

title: 3. Blood data with bloodstream
text:
Start the app
To keep the commands short, first save two paths in variables. If you open a new terminal, run these two lines again:
DATA=/neurodesktop-storage/course-material/pet/data/ds004869
SIF=/neurodesktop-storage/course-material/pet/containers
Then start bloodstream:
cd ~/pet_course
apptainer run -B $DATA:/data:ro $SIF/bloodstream.sif --mode interactive --bids_dir /data --derivatives_dir ~/pet_course/derivatives
What the command does:

apptainer run ... $SIF/bloodstream.sif runs the bloodstream container.
-B $DATA:/data:ro makes the dataset visible inside the container as /data, read-only.
--bids_dir /data tells bloodstream where the BIDS data are.
--derivatives_dir ~/pet_course/derivatives tells bloodstream where to write its results: your own folder.

You can ignore these messages:

INFO: Environment variable SINGULARITYENV_MATLABPATH is set...
WARNING: While bind mounting '/data:/data': destination is already in the mount point list

title: 3. Blood data with bloodstream
text:
Open the app
Wait until the terminal shows Listening on http://0.0.0.0:3838. Then open a new browser tab with your Neurodesk link, and replace everything after your port number with /proxy/3838/:
http://130.238.147.132:YOUR_PORT/proxy/3838/
The final / is needed. If the terminal says a different port, such as 3839, use that number instead.

title: 3. Blood data with bloodstream
text:
Run a default analysis

Restrict the analysis to the six workshop participants: 02;05;08;11;13;14.
Leave all the other settings as they are, and run the pipeline from the app. Keep the app’s tab open until the app closes itself.

The run takes several minutes, and its progress appears in the terminal.
The results are in ~/pet_course/derivatives/bloodstream/Primary_Analysis. Open the report, bloodstream_report.html, in JupyterLab, and click Trust HTML at the top, which turns on the interactive plots.

What did the default settings do with each blood component?
Do the curves look reasonable for every participant?

title: 3. Blood data with bloodstream
text:
Build your own models
Start the app again, with one extra option, --analysis_foldername, so that the new results go to a separate folder and don’t replace the default analysis:
cd ~/pet_course
apptainer run -B $DATA:/data:ro $SIF/bloodstream.sif --mode interactive --bids_dir /data --derivatives_dir ~/pet_course/derivatives --analysis_foldername Secondary_Analysis

Open the app as before.
Restrict the analysis to the six workshop participants: 02;05;08;11;13;14.
Choose a model for each blood component.
Run the pipeline, and keep the tab open until the app closes itself.

The results are in ~/pet_course/derivatives/bloodstream/Secondary_Analysis. Open the report and click Trust HTML.

Do the model fits look reasonable for every participant?
How do the results differ from the default analysis?

title: 5. Lassen plot
text:
Celecoxib blocks COX-2. A Lassen plot estimates how much of the target the drug occupies, using VT from the baseline and blocked scans.
For each participant and region:
If the drug occupies the same fraction of the target in every region, and the non-displaceable distribution volume (VND) is the same in every region, the points fall on a straight line. The slope of the line is the occupancy, and the line crosses the x-axis at VND.

title: 5. Lassen plot
text:
Your task
Make a Lassen plot for each participant in the blocking group, and estimate the occupancy and VND.

Use the VT estimates from MA1 or Logan, from your Lassen analysis.
PETFit saves the estimates for each model in ~/pet_course/derivatives/petfit/Lassen_Analysis, in files that end in _kinpar.tsv. The file at the top of that folder combines all participants and regions.
Work in a Jupyter notebook: in the Launcher, click Python 3. The pandas and matplotlib packages are installed.

title: 5. Lassen plot
text:
Questions

Do your estimates agree between participants, and between MA1 and Logan?
Which regions fall close to the line, and which don’t? Why might that be?
What assumptions does a Lassen plot make, and are they reasonable here?

title: Before you start
text:
If your Neurodesk from the fMRI workshop is still running, open its link and skip to Open a terminal.

Connect to the Uppsala University VPN.
In a terminal on your laptop, log in to the course server with your Akka ID:
ssh AKKA_ID@130.238.147.132
Start the course Neurodesk:
neurodesk_hfbi
Copy the link that it prints, which starts with http://130.238.147.132:, and open it in your browser. ezBIDS officially supports Chrome and Edge, but Firefox works too.







ImportantKeep your link



The number after 130.238.147.132: is your personal port number, and you need it later to open the apps. If you lose the link, run neurodesk_hfbi again on the server: if your Neurodesk is already running, it prints the link again without restarting anything.


The link also logs you in. The end of the link, ?token=..., works like a password, and the browser that opens the link remembers it. Use that same browser for the whole workshop. If you open one of the apps in a different browser, you see a page that says “Token authentication is enabled”. To fix it, open your full link in that browser first.

title: Before you start
text:
Open a terminal
In JupyterLab, open the Launcher tab and click Terminal. You type most commands in this terminal. Paste with Ctrl+V, or Ctrl+Shift+V if that doesn’t work.

title: Before you start
text:
Set up your working folder
Run the setup script once:
/neurodesktop-storage/course-material/pet/scripts/setup_pet_course.sh
The script creates the folder ~/pet_course/derivatives and copies the PETPrep outputs that you need into it (about 12 MB).






TipTab completion



Type the first few letters of each part of a path and press Tab to complete it. This saves typing and avoids typos.

title: 3. Blood data with bloodstream
text:
Fit models to the data
Start the app again, with one extra option, --analysis_foldername, so that the new results go to a separate folder and don’t replace the default analysis:
cd ~/pet_course
apptainer run -B $DATA:/data:ro $SIF/bloodstream.sif --mode interactive --bids_dir /data --derivatives_dir ~/pet_course/derivatives --analysis_foldername Secondary_Analysis

Open the app as before.
Restrict the analysis to the six workshop participants: 02;05;08;11;13;14.
Choose a model for the parent fraction, the blood-to-plasma ratio, and the arterial input function. What do the options mean, and which would you choose for each?
Run the pipeline, and keep the tab open until the app closes itself.

The results are in ~/pet_course/derivatives/bloodstream/Secondary_Analysis. Open the report and click Trust HTML.

Do the model fits look reasonable for every participant?
